title: Devanagari
hook: the bar along the top of the letters: what it holds up, and the last few days held up the same way
tomorrow: why is one vowel written before the letter it's sounded after?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Devanagari, and akshara: a letter, and also what doesn't wear away. Among letters, Krishna says, I am a. Today, a look back along the line.

Fairy lights strung along a balcony. Shirts pegged on a clothesline. Charms on a bracelet. Take away the line and it's just a pile. So, yesterday's question: what is the bar across the top of Devanagari holding up? A word. The bar is called the shirorekha, the head line, and the letters of one word hang from it together. Where the bar breaks, one word ends and the next begins. In English a space does that job. In Devanagari, the line does it too.
screen: `TAKE AWAY THE LINE: A PILE.` → `THE SHIROREKHA, THE HEAD LINE.` → `WHERE IT BREAKS, A NEW WORD.`

segments.voice: So a new reader's first move isn't sounding out every letter. It's finding the bars. Count them, and you've counted the words before you can read a single one. Then go left to right, like English, one letter at a time, each with its short a inside unless a small mark takes it away. That's how a wall of shapes starts turning into words. Now hold the last few days up the same way, each on its own short bar. Savitri, talking with Death on the road. Gargi, asking what the world is woven on, and coming back with more questions when she was told to stop. The Varkaris, carrying their saints' sandals to Pandharpur. The hymn of creation, ending on perhaps. Vyasa, asking his scribe to understand every line before writing it down. And yesterday's akshara: a letter, and the imperishable. Separate words, one line running across them: people asking out loud, walking together, keeping their words. That line is where a reader starts.
screen: `FIND THE BARS FIRST.` · `LEFT TO RIGHT, A INSIDE EACH LETTER.` · `THE LAST FEW DAYS, WORD BY WORD.` · then, large: `ONE LINE RUNNING ACROSS THEM.`

segments.voice: Count, on your fingers, the people who taught you to read: a parent, a teacher, an older cousin with a picture book, whoever it was. One finger and one slow breath for each. If one of them also taught you a prayer, a song or a story, stay with that one a little longer.
Devanagari, still: letters hanging together from one head line, read left to right. Year five's word for a while yet.
Hold on to it: Devanagari, where the line shows you the word. Two days into year five.

howItsDone: People learning Devanagari often start by copying letters under a ruled top line, and teachers point out the bar first so a learner can see where each word begins and ends.
